title: Fire rescue expansion funding and Milford Avenue subdivision
subtitle: Four-unit housing consultation, culture plan report, former mayor's FCM award, and mosquito larvicide permission.
overview: Council released $1,000,000 in Development Charges funding for feasibility and architectural design work on the Fire Rescue Expansion project, and directed staff to hire a consulting firm for the design work {{vote:m4}}. Council also endorsed a draft plan of subdivision for 91-97 Milford Avenue {{vote:m5}}. It is a technical first step that would allow the centre townhouse block to be sold as condominiums while the existing rental townhouses stay rental.

Council received the annual culture plan report card and agreed to keep championing local cultural development {{vote:m2}}. It also authorized the Mayor to sign a letter permitting the Region of Waterloo to apply larvicide on city-owned land {{vote:m6}}. The annual statement of remuneration and expenses for elected officials was received as information {{vote:m3}}.

In an informal public meeting, staff outlined a possible zoning change to allow four-unit housing across the city. No decision was made. Staff expect to return to Council in the fall, and councillors asked for wider public engagement. The meeting also included a presentation of the FCM Ann MacLean Award to the family of former mayor Lynne Woolstencroft. A closed session was held earlier in the afternoon.

decisions.detail: Council released $1,000,000 from the 2024-2026 Capital Budget, funded from the Development Charges Fund, for feasibility and architectural design work, and directed staff to retain a consulting firm for design.

decisions.item: Milford Avenue draft plan of subdivision
decisions.detail: Council endorsed Draft Plan of Subdivision 30T-23410 for 91-97 Milford Avenue, delegated authority for administrative changes to standard conditions, and authorized the Mayor and Clerk to sign the subdivision agreement.
Council received report CAO2024-003 and agreed to continue championing local cultural development.
The Mayor was authorized to sign a letter of permission allowing larvicide to be applied on city-owned lands as part of the Region's West Nile Virus program.
Council received the annual statement of remuneration and expenses for elected officials (CORP2024-009) as information.

debate: On four-unit housing, councillors asked how stable low-density neighbourhoods would be protected and whether changes would be allowed as of right, skipping a planning process. One councillor said the change could allow infill on nearly every residential lot and suggested mock-ups showing what four-storey buildings would look like.

Several councillors raised how to reach residents across the whole city. Staff said they would add a communications campaign to the online engagement page. Another councillor cautioned that feedback should also reflect future residents who cannot yet afford to live in Waterloo.

A councillor asked whether the rules would be feasible in practice, noting that height limits, parking and floor-area caps could make new units impractical. Staff said they would review the barriers applicants have faced. Staff also said displacement is hard to address through zoning.

A delegate supported four-unit housing but called the timeline to fall 2024 too slow. The delegate urged incremental steps and relaxing parking minimums. Staff clarified that the timeline is counted from the October 2023 direction.

On Milford Avenue, councillors asked how renters would be affected by the common-element condominium. The applicant's consultant said tenants would keep their current rental arrangements and the landlord would carry any condominium fees. Staff said converting the rentals would need vacancy-rate thresholds met and a Council decision.
